title: Do you remember when we thought about curriculum?
author: Claire Stoneman
summary: Claire Stoneman, a veteran English teacher in a high-poverty English school, laments that day-to-day educational discourse has drifted away from curriculum since the thoughtful, subject-rich years of 2019 to 2021. She argues that curriculum is the lifeblood of a school and that knowledge, as Newman put it, is an acquired illumination that lets pupils see, judge and create. She worries that schools are sliding toward fads, plug-and-play slide decks and purchased programmes that supply classroom moves without any curriculum thought. Against American models where AI apps and guides let students supposedly crush academics in two hours, she defends subjects as places to linger, and teachers as humans who know their pupils. She concedes that some learning is boring and onerous, using her opera training to show that automaticity frees working memory for higher thinking. The urgency is greatest in her school, where over 70 percent of pupils receive the Pupil Premium and deserve induction into their intellectual inheritance.
points: Curriculum, defined as what a school thinks important enough to stay with children for life, should be the centre of school discourse, and she sees it being displaced by fads and pet projects.
Purchased programmes and slide decks give teachers classroom moves without curriculum thought, hollowing out the subject itself.
Using her opera experience, she argues that repeated, sometimes boring practice builds automaticity that frees working memory for deeper thinking.
Compressing subjects into a two-hour AI-app routine with no teachers removes thought, beauty and agency, and replaces a human who knows the child with an algorithm.
Disadvantaged pupils most need a knowledge-rich induction into their subjects, since it is their birthright and collective inheritance.
quotes: And yet curriculum is the lifeblood of a school. It is literally what we think is important enough that our children should learn and take away with them when they leave at age 11, 16 or 18.
Knowledge illuminates. It helps one to see, judge, understand, evaluate. It shines a light on the subject itself enabling pupils to think, challenge, create.
You can buy a programme for a few thousand quid that will give you the classroom moves without the curriculum thought. Plug and play slide subject decks to click through. Manuals abound.
Our subjects are not for a two hour grab and go. They are to wander in, to think, to question, to talk about, to wonder.
Sometimes learning is boring. When I was singing a lot of opera I had to go over the same bar of coloratura in a Mozart aria again and again and again before I could master it.
If we dump anything taxing or hard or difficult into an app, what’s left? No thought. No beauty. No agency.

And I want the children in my school to be taught by a human being who understands their quirks and idiosyncrasies and all the messiness of being a child and a teenager, who knows them as a human not an algorithm, and teaches them their subject for all that they are worth.
I’ll be damned if they’re not inducted into the subjects that are their birth right, their collective inheritance; knowledge, in the words of St John Henry Newman, as being of itself a treasure.
context: She frames curriculum as the central purpose of a school, which is why its fading from discourse troubles her.
Newman's image of knowledge as light is her basis for saying subject knowledge enables independent thought.
She criticises bought-in programmes that supply teaching moves while skipping the intellectual work of curriculum design.
She contrasts the lingering, exploratory nature of a subject with fast AI-driven models of schooling.
A personal opera anecdote shows that tedious repetition is a legitimate stage on the way to mastery.
Offloading difficulty to an app, she argues, strips learning of thought, beauty and the learner's own agency.
Her case for human teachers rests on their knowing each child as a person rather than a data point.
She makes the equity argument that poorer pupils are the ones who most need induction into their subjects.
